items.text: Trump, Xi and Putin issued a joint "peace declaration" after their first three-way meeting, pledging U.N. reform and that nuclear war "must never be fought," with no arms-control deal.
items.detail: The leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers met for about 90 minutes in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday local time (Wednesday evening ET) on the sidelines of the APEC summit, after Trump held separate meetings with Xi and Putin. The four-point declaration, posted by the White House, says the three will reform the U.N., increase production and supply of refined petroleum products, respect the immunity of state officials (saying the International Criminal Court and similar bodies "must not abuse their jurisdiction"), and hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the spread of nuclear weapons. It sets no limits on any country's arsenal. Putin did not commit to attending the G20 summit in Miami next month, Reuters reported. Trump then left China for Washington.
items.why: It is the first summit of the three nuclear superpowers' leaders, but it produced pledges rather than binding commitments.

items.text: Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, the U.N.'s top court ruled Thursday, the first time it has found a country itself responsible for genocide.
items.detail: The International Court of Justice found that Myanmar's security forces intentionally killed Rohingya, caused them serious bodily or mental harm and imposed measures meant to prevent births during the 2017 "clearance operations" in northern Rakhine state, and that Myanmar failed to prevent and punish genocide. The court cited an estimated 10,000 Rohingya killed; about 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. It ordered Myanmar to investigate and prosecute those responsible, allow safe return of displaced Rohingya, and compensate them, with the amount to be set later; Myanmar must report back within two years. The judgment in the case brought by The Gambia in 2019 is final, binding and without appeal. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed it.
items.why: It is the first time the world court has held a state directly responsible for committing genocide.

items.text: President Trump said the U.S. will "see what happens" with Iran after Jan. 1, a day after warning "we'll wipe them out" if Iran set off a dirty bomb in Washington.
items.detail: Trump did not explain the significance of Jan. 1 in the interview broadcast Thursday, Reuters reported. On Wednesday, asked about a reported Iranian dirty-bomb plot, he said residents of Washington need not panic but that the U.S. would "wipe them out" if it happened, and said there was an indication Iran was "looking at" gases and biological weapons, without giving evidence. Trump has alternated between threatening escalation and suggesting he could wind down the nine-month war. Israel has passed intelligence to the U.S. on Iran's military buildup, officials told Reuters.
items.why: Trump is signaling a possible deadline in a war that has U.S. forces trading fire with Iran again.

items.text: Denmark's parliament unanimously approved the U.S.-Denmark-Greenland security pact Thursday, opening the way to a bigger U.S. military role in Greenland.
items.detail: The vote was 109-0, U.S. Ambassador Ken Howery said. The deal, signed in September by Trump and the Danish and Greenlandic prime ministers and already approved by Greenland's parliament, updates a 1951 defense agreement to give the U.S. underwater access and permission to build a missile-defense system, and says Greenland would stay in NATO if it became independent. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen said the last step before it takes effect is a U.S. notification to Congress, and that the U.S. has not yet told Denmark of plans for new bases. Trump had threatened earlier this year to take control of the island.
items.why: It settles months of conflict between the U.S. and a NATO ally over Trump's demands for Greenland.

items.text: Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, raising about $81 billion in the largest stock offering ever and valuing the AI company near $1.5 trillion.
items.detail: The maker of the Claude AI models sold 980 million shares, above its planned $70-$78 range and more than the 825 million first offered, AP reported; the proceeds top SpaceX's roughly $75 billion IPO in June. Shares begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Anthropic said it had $33.24 billion in revenue in the first nine months of 2026, and a net loss of $104 billion, most of it from accounting changes on convertible notes and other instruments, CNBC reported.
items.why: The size of the debut is a test of investor appetite for AI after weeks of selling in chip and tech stocks.

items.text: Almost all Fed officials expect more interest-rate increases will likely be needed, minutes of their October meeting showed.
items.detail: At the Oct. 27-28 meeting, 10 members voted to hold the federal funds rate at 3.75% to 4%; Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Almost all participants judged that further increases would likely be appropriate to bring inflation back to 2%, and a couple said a hike larger than a quarter point could be considered at the Dec. 8-9 meeting if inflation data were unfavorable. Almost all also discussed the risk that returns on AI investment disappoint investors. The S&P 500 fell for a fifth straight day Wednesday, its longest losing streak since June, and the Dow dropped 561 points, AP reported.
items.why: Higher rates would raise borrowing costs on mortgages, car loans and credit cards.

items.text: The U.S. and Venezuela signed a deal restoring military ties for the first time in 21 years, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in Caracas.
items.detail: Hegseth, the highest-ranking U.S. official to visit since U.S. forces captured Nicolás Maduro on Jan. 3, met acting President Delcy Rodríguez. He said the agreement covers joint training, intelligence sharing, equipment and efforts to strengthen Venezuela's military, and cooperation against criminal and terrorist groups. Officials did not say whether it allows U.S. bases or permanent troop deployments, and its full terms were not released. Hugo Chávez cut defense ties with Washington in 2005.
items.why: It turns a former adversary into a U.S. security partner less than a year after Maduro's removal.

items.text: Flooding from more than 15 inches of rain swamped parts of South Florida, collapsing a synagogue roof and closing schools in Broward and Miami-Dade.
items.detail: Hollywood, Sunrise and Plantation in Broward County got more than 15 inches over 72 hours. The roof of Temple Sinai in Hollywood collapsed early Wednesday; no one was hurt. State wildlife officers rescued more than 70 residents from a flooded Hollywood apartment complex, and I-95 ramps and Florida's Turnpike flooded. Broward and Miami-Dade public schools were closed Thursday, and a flood watch with 2 to 4 more inches possible ran through Thursday evening, CBS Miami reported.
items.why: Residents across the Miami-Fort Lauderdale area faced flooded roads and homes and closed schools.

week.text: Measles is formally no longer eliminated in the U.S., Mexico and Bolivia, the Pan American Health Organization announced Tuesday, after a year of nonstop spread.
week.detail: PAHO Director Jarbas Barbosa accepted the finding of the regional commission that met Nov. 10-13: the same measles strain circulated for 12 months or more in each country, with the U.S. reaching that mark on Jan. 20, 2026, Mexico on Feb. 1 and Bolivia on April 16. The U.S. had held elimination status for 26 years. The Americas have reported 58,213 confirmed cases and 82 deaths this year through Nov. 13, versus 12,806 cases a year earlier; the U.S. has more than 5,400 cases, its highest annual total since the 1989-91 resurgence, UNICEF said, 96% in unvaccinated people or those of unknown status. Canada lost its status in November 2025. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said the U.S. will work to regain the status and that he recommends the MMR vaccine.
week.why: It is official recognition that measles is again spreading continuously in the U.S.

week.text: Online banking at Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and other big U.S. banks failed for thousands of customers Monday; Chase blamed a technical issue, not a cyberattack.
week.detail: Customers began reporting trouble Monday morning, and by 2 p.m. ET nearly 4,800 users had reported problems with Chase on Downdetector, the most of any bank, including balances, transfers, wires and check deposits. Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, Truist and Capital One customers also reported problems. "Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds," Chase said. U.S. Bank said its systems were not directly hit but Zelle transfers with other banks could be delayed; Capital One said it was operating normally; Zelle said its network was working and that a problem at Chase may be delaying payments. A Justice Department official told MS NOW there was no evidence of an attack. No full restoration had been announced by publish time.
week.why: Millions of Americans rely on these banks for paychecks, bills and transfers, days after FAA and Microsoft outages.

week.text: A new Commerce Department rule bars China and other restricted countries from reaching advanced U.S. AI chips remotely through data centers abroad.
week.detail: The Bureau of Industry and Security issued the interim final rule Monday, saying it was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council. Companies now need licenses to export, reexport or transfer advanced AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere that may provide computing power to companies based in China, Russia, Iran, North Korea or other embargoed (D:5) countries, including through brokers; it covers sites above about 12 million TPP, roughly 750 Nvidia H100-class chips. It also adds license requirements for advanced chip shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, except to U.S.-based companies, gives existing data-center operators 90 days to get licenses, and formally rescinds the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. It comes days after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.
week.why: It closes the main loophole Chinese AI firms used to tap American chips and puts new paperwork on data centers worldwide.

upcoming.detail: Release date per the Conference Board. The index rose 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, up from 84.2 in September.
